segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When this brought Paul and Barnabas into no small conflict and debate with them, they arranged for Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them to go up to Jerusalem, to the apostles and elders, about this question.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, sent on their way by the assembly, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, telling in detail of the conversion of the Gentiles, and they brought great joy to all the brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all that God had done with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some from the party of the Pharisees who had believed stood up and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is necessary to circumcise them and to command them to keep the Law of Moses.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The apostles and the elders gathered to look into this matter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After much debate, Peter stood up and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the good news and believe.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So now why are you putting God to the test by laying on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we have had the strength to bear?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: No, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they are.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The whole community fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul recounting all the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had fallen silent, James replied,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Brothers, listen to me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Simeon has recounted how God first concerned himself to take from the Gentiles a people for his name.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And with this the words of the prophets agree, as it is written:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: ‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David; I will rebuild its ruins and set it upright again,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles over whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who makes these things

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: known from of old.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Therefore I judge that we should not make difficulties for those from the Gentiles who are turning to God,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: but should write to them to abstain from things polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For Moses from ancient generations has had in every city those who proclaim him, since he is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the apostles and the elders, together with the whole assembly, resolved to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They wrote this to be delivered by their hand:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers from among the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia: Greetings.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Since we have heard that some who went out from us have disturbed you with their words and unsettled your minds, though we gave them no instructions,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: we have resolved, having come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So we have sent Judas and Silas, who will themselves tell you the same things by word of mouth.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For the Holy Spirit and we have resolved to lay on you no further burden than these necessary things:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: to abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, and after gathering the community they delivered the letter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they read it, they rejoiced at the encouragement.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judas and Silas, who were themselves also prophets, encouraged the brothers at length and strengthened them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After spending some time there, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and, along with many others, bringing the good news of the word of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come, let us go back and visit the brothers in every city where we announced the word of the Lord, and see how they are doing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Barnabas wanted to take along John, called Mark, as well,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but Paul thought it right not to take along this man, who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them to the work.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disagreement became so sharp that they parted from each other: Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: while Paul chose Silas and set out, entrusted by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He passed through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. “Church” remains the near-universal rendering, and readers should understand “assembly” here as the community of believers, not a single meeting.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations,” and in the plural in Jewish usage it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses “Gentiles” for that sense and “nations” elsewhere, but it is one word. In verse 14 James plays on it: God takes from the “nations” a “people,” the term normally reserved for Israel.
“Gospel” is now a religious term or a book title; the Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for Israel testing God in the wilderness. “Tempt” in modern English means to entice to sin, which is not the idea here; most recent versions also use “test.”
This is a Semitic form of the name Simon and refers to Simon Peter, who has just spoken. The form suits a speaker from the Aramaic-speaking community in Jerusalem.

The verb is the Septuagint’s regular word for God “visiting” his people to act for them. Here it has no personal object and is completed by “to take a people,” so “visited” would require supplying words. English versions divide between “visited the Gentiles,” “concerned himself,” “looked favorably,” and “intervened.”

The Greek is the ordinary word for a tent or hut. The image is of David’s royal house as a collapsed shelter that God will rebuild. Older versions have “tabernacle”; several modern ones already use “tent” or “dwelling.”

notes.phrase: so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord
notes.traditional: that the residue of men might seek after the Lord
notes.note: James quotes Amos 9:11–12 in a form close to the ancient Greek translation, with some wording that differs from it. The Hebrew text of Amos reads differently here: “that they may possess the remnant of Edom.” The Greek version, with all humanity seeking the Lord, is the one that carries James’s argument.

notes.phrase: over whom my name has been called
notes.traditional: who are called by my name
notes.note: The Greek reproduces a Hebrew idiom in which calling one’s name over something marks it as one’s own property. The traditional rendering suggests only that the Gentiles bear God’s name; the idiom says they belong to him.

notes.traditional: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world
notes.note: The words can be read as “who makes these things known from of old” or as “who does these things, which have been known from of old”; the translation allows the first and the Greek permits either. Many later manuscripts expand the phrase into a separate sentence, which the King James Version follows; the shorter text is generally judged original.

This refers to meat from animals killed without draining the blood. The four prohibitions are often thought to echo the rules that Leviticus 17–18 lays on foreigners living among Israel, though this is debated; others see them as matters associated with pagan worship. Some manuscripts of the Western tradition omit “what has been strangled” here and in verse 29 and add a negative form of the Golden Rule, turning the list into moral rules.

The Greek expression, used here and in verses 25 and 28, is the standard formula with which Greek cities and councils recorded official decisions. “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (verse 28) is the familiar rendering and is literal, but in English it sounds tentative where the Greek states a formal resolution.

The Greek word covers a person’s life and inner self. Here it is the seat of conviction that the visitors have unsettled, for which “minds” is the natural English; most modern versions agree. The same word is rendered “lives” in verse 26.

The verb ordinarily means “hand over.” With “their lives” as object, most translations understand it as exposing their lives to danger, but it can also be read as “devoted their lives.” The same verb appears in verse 40, where the brothers hand Paul over to the Lord’s grace, rendered there “entrusted.”

notes.phrase: to those who had sent them
notes.note: Verse 34 (“But it seemed good to Silas to remain there”) is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not part of the Greek text translated here. It was probably added by copyists to explain how Silas could be in Antioch in verse 40.

candidates.reason: The plural for community members recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translators divide between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters,” and “believers.”
Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul, and Revelation, with versions varying between “fornication,” “sexual immorality,” “unchastity,” and “prostitution.”
The plural for Israel’s forebears is frequent in Acts, Paul, and Hebrews, and “fathers” versus “ancestors” should be settled once.
The noun and its verb παρακαλέω range over encourage, comfort, exhort, and appeal, and need a governed split so the cognate link stays visible.
A core term across the New Testament where “grace,” “favor,” and “gift” compete and a reader would be misled by unexplained variation.

warnings: Verse 26: ψυχή is not rendered with a register form (life; soul; person / people / everyone / human being; living being / living creature; mind; wholeheartedly; keep in suspense) and has no register-exception note.
Verse 14: ἐπισκέπτομαι is not rendered with a register form (visit; look after; care for; concern oneself; look for / select / pick out) and has no register-exception note.
